xu.summary: The preface describes the setting and buildings of the Palace of Nine Perfections, then praises Emperor Taizong's frugality: he built nothing new but only mended the old Sui palace. It ends with the finding of a sweet spring in the fourth month of the sixth year of Zhenguan, when the Emperor guided the water out with his staff while walking with the Empress, and cites the classics to show that a sweet spring is an auspicious sign of his virtue.
xu.translation:
In the fourth month, early summer, of the sixth year of Zhenguan, the Emperor withdrew from the summer heat to the Palace of Nine Perfections, which was the Renshou Palace of the Sui. It crowns the mountain and raises its halls, cuts across ravines to make pools, spans the water with pillars and splits the cliffs with gate towers. High pavilions were built all round, long corridors rise on every side, ridgepoles and eaves interlock, and terraces and kiosks rise and fall unevenly. Looking up, it soars far for a hundred fathoms; looking down, it towers a thousand fathoms. Pearls and jade answer one another, gold and blue-green shine together, dazzling the clouds and hiding the sun and moon. Seeing how they moved hills and turned streams, went to the limit of lavishness and excess, and made men serve desire, one may well blame them deeply. Yet when the blazing sun melts gold there is no sultry steam here, and when a faint wind stirs slowly there is a chill coolness. It is truly a fine place to rest the body, a splendid place to nourish the spirit. Even the Ganquan palace of the Han could not surpass it.

The Emperor, at twenty, was already laying plans for the four quarters; by thirty he was cherishing and ruling hundreds of millions. He began by uniting all within the seas through arms, and ended by winning the far-off peoples with civil virtue. To the east he crossed Qingqiu, to the south he went beyond the red frontier, and all brought rare gifts and offerings, and came to pay homage through relays of interpreters. To the west as far as Luntai, to the north holding back the Dark Gate, all these lands were set out as prefectures and counties and their people filled the registers. The qi was pure and the years were harmonious; the near was at peace and the far was respectful; all beings fulfilled themselves, and every spiritual blessing arrived. Though this relied on the work of Heaven and Earth, in the end it depended on the thought of one man. Forgetting himself for the good of all things, combed by the wind and bathed by the rain, with the people always in his heart, he wore himself with worry into illness. His flesh was dry as dried meat like Yao's, and his feet were callused worse than Yu's. Needles and stones were applied again and again, and still the pores stayed blocked.

When he lived in the capital he suffered every year from the summer heat, and his subjects begged him to build a detached palace, hoping he could ease his spirit and nourish his nature. But the Sage on high cherished the labour of a single man and spared the property of ten households; he shut the matter tight, refused, and would not yield. He considered that the Sui palace had been built in an earlier age; to abandon it would be a waste, to pull it down would be heavy labour; in affairs the main thing is to follow what exists, so why must one build anew? So he cut carving back to the plain, and then cut again and again; he removed what was too lavish and mended what had fallen into ruin. He mixed gravel into the red courtyard and broke the whitewashed walls with mud plaster; jade steps join earthen stairs, and thatch continues the jewelled rooms. Looking up, the grandeur could serve as a warning drawn from the past; looking down, the humility and frugality are enough to leave a lesson for descendants. This is what is meant by: the perfect man does not act, the great sage does not make; others exhaust their strength, and I enjoy the fruit.

Now the ponds of old all drew from valley streams, but within the palace city there was no source of water, and seeking one found none. It depended on a single thing, which was not something human strength could bring about, and yet the sage's heart kept it in mind and did not forget. On the sixteenth day, the jihai day, of the fourth month, the month which began on the jiashen day, the Emperor and the Empress went round the terraces and halls, strolled in the shade of the west side of the city, and paused beneath a high pavilion. Looking down at the ground, he noticed that it was slightly damp. He guided it with his staff; a spring welled up as he did so, and he received it in a stone trough and led it into a single channel. It was clear as a mirror and sweet as fine wine. To the south it pours past the right side of the Danxiao hall, to the east it flows across the twin gate towers. It threads through the blue-patterned doors and winds about the purple chambers. It stirs clear waves and washes away blemish and filth. It can guide and nourish one's true nature, and clarify and brighten the heart and spirit. It mirrors all forms and moistens all things that live. Like a deep kindness that never runs dry, like a dark grace that always flows, it is not only the essence of the images of Heaven, but also a treasure of the spirits of Earth.

I respectfully note that the Weft on the Rites says: "When a king punishes and kills according to the crime, rewards according to merit, and fits the rites, a sweet spring comes forth in the palace gate." The Heguanzi says: "When the sage's virtue reaches up to the great purity, down to the great peace, and through to the myriad spirits, a sweet spring comes forth." The Diagram of Auspicious Responses says: "When a king is purely harmonious and his food and drink are not tribute, a sweet spring comes forth, and whoever drinks it lives long." The Dongguan Han Records says: "In the first year of Zhongyuan of Emperor Guangwu, a sweet spring came forth in the capital, and all who drank from it were cured of long-standing illness." So the arrival of this divine thing is truly to support a bright sage; it can clear away that deep-rooted illness, and will also lengthen the years.

Therefore the hundred lords and ministers hurried forward with changed faces. Our lord, holding to his humility, pushed it away and would not own it. Though blessed, he does not count himself blessed: this is not heard only of the past; to fear what is auspicious is truly proved in the present. This is the dark token of Heaven on high and the fine virtue of the Son of Heaven; how could my shallow learning make it fully known? But my office is to record words, and this belongs to the record of events; I cannot let the splendour of the state be left out of the canons and registers. I dare to set down a true account, and so I carve this inscription.

keyLines.line: 維貞觀六年孟夏之月，皇帝避暑乎九成之宮，此則隨之仁壽宮也
keyLines.en: In the fourth month, early summer, of the sixth year of Zhenguan, the Emperor withdrew from the summer heat to the Palace of Nine Perfections, which was the Renshou Palace of the Sui
keyLines.note: The opening gives the time and place: in the fourth month of 632 the Emperor spent the summer at Jiuchenggong, formerly the Renshou Palace of the Sui dynasty (581-618).

keyLines.line: 珠璧交映，金碧相輝，照灼雲霞，蔽虧日月
keyLines.en: Pearls and jade answer one another, gold and blue-green shine together, dazzling the clouds and hiding the sun and moon
keyLines.note: Describes the splendour of the palace, glittering against the clouds and the sun and moon.

keyLines.line: 於是斲彫為樸，損之又損，去其泰甚，葺其頹壞
keyLines.en: So he cut carving back to the plain, and then cut again and again; he removed what was too lavish and mended what had fallen into ruin
keyLines.note: Praises Taizong for choosing the simple over the ornate when he repaired the old palace, and for sparing the people's labour.

keyLines.line: 粵以四月甲申朔旬有六日己亥，上及中宮，歷覽臺觀
keyLines.en: On the sixteenth day, the jihai day, of the fourth month, the Emperor and the Empress went round the terraces and halls
keyLines.note: A precise record of when the spring was found: the sixteenth of the fourth month, while the Emperor and Empress were touring the palace grounds.

keyLines.line: 因而以杖導之，有泉隨而涌出，乃承以石檻，引為一渠
keyLines.en: He guided it with his staff; a spring welled up as he did so, and he received it in a stone trough and led it into a single channel
keyLines.note: How the sweet spring was found: Taizong guided the ground with his staff, water welled up, and a stone channel was built.

keyLines.en: It was clear as a mirror and sweet as fine wine
keyLines.note: Describes the clearness and sweetness of the water.

keyLines.line: 斯乃上帝玄符，天子令德，豈臣之末學，所能丕顯
keyLines.en: This is the dark token of Heaven on high and the fine virtue of the Son of Heaven; how could my shallow learning make it fully known?
keyLines.note: Wei Zheng modestly says that his learning is too slight to bring out the Emperor's great virtue.

keyLines.en: I dare to set down a true account, and so I carve this inscription
keyLines.note: Explains the purpose of the stele: the inscription is written from a faithful record.

glossary.note: The first month of summer, the fourth lunar month.
A detached palace built by Emperor Wen of the Sui; the Tang dynasty (618-907) renamed it Jiuchenggong. It lies in today's Linyou county in Shaanxi.
A spring of water as sweet as sweet wine, which the ancients saw as a lucky sign.

glossary.en: yi shen li wu - forgetting oneself for the good of things
glossary.note: To give no thought to oneself and to work for the benefit of others.

glossary.en: Li wei, Heguanzi, Ruiying tu - the Weft on the Rites, the Heguanzi and the Diagram of Auspicious Responses
glossary.note: All ancient books that record lucky omens; Wei Zheng cites them to show that the sweet spring is a sign of a ruler's good government.
The site of Jiuchenggong, in today's Shaanxi.

xu.background: In the sixth year of Zhenguan (632), Emperor Taizong of the Tang found a spring while escaping the heat at the Palace of Nine Perfections. Wei Zheng wrote the text on imperial command and Ouyang Xun wrote it out for the carvers, and a stele was raised in memory. This stele is called the 'finest regular script under Heaven'. Its characters are square and dignified with tight structure, and it is one of the most important models for learning regular script.

ming.summary: The inscription is in four-character rhymed lines. It praises Taizong for achievements that surpass those of Yao, Shun and Yu, and honours the sweet spring as a lucky sign sent down from Heaven; at the same time it stresses that the Emperor stays alert in times of peace and prizes plainness, warning rulers to keep what is full without letting it overflow.
ming.translation:
August is the one who holds the turning fortunes,
and in an instant unites the whole world.
A thousand years awaited this appointed time,
and now all things behold it.
His merit stands higher than the great Shun,
his diligence runs deeper than Yu the Great.
Without equal before him, and none to follow,
he climbs past the Three and goes beyond the Five.
Gripping the pivot and treading the square,
he is holy and he is divine.
By arms he overcame disaster and disorder;
by culture he cherished those from afar.
Where writing and tally-marks had never reached,
and none had ever bowed in homage,
caps and robes now follow one another
and gifts of treasure are all displayed.
The great Way has no name;
supreme virtue does not call itself virtue.
Hidden works turn in the dark,
their springs so deep they cannot be fathomed.
People dig wells and drink,
plough fields and eat;
they have no thanks for Heaven's work,
so how would they know the Emperor's power?
What Heaven carries
has no smell and no sound.
The ten thousand kinds take their beginning from it,
and things flow into form.
They change their substance as they are moved
and answer virtue with spirit.
Sudden as an echo,
brilliant and bright.
A throng of blessings gathers,
a rich abundance of good fortune:
the cloud lord and the dragon officials,
the tortoise chart and the phoenix chronicle;
the sun holds five colours
and the crow shows three toes.
The hymns never rest from their work,
and the historian's brush does not stop.
The highest goodness sends down omens;
the highest wisdom is glad of them.
Humility flows and moistens what lies below,
murmuring, bright and pure.
It has the taste of duckweed and sweet wine,
it is ice set hard, a mirror made clear.
Use it and it is new each day;
draw from it and it never runs dry.
The Way follows the season and is at ease;
good fortune flows with the spring.
Our lord is wary even at night
and, though blessed, does not count himself blessed.
He lives beneath a lofty thatch
and takes no pleasure in roaming.
The yellow-roofed carriage is no honour to him;
the worry of the world is his.
Others toy with the show;
he takes the substance.
He turns back to simplicity and to the root,
and puts plainness in place of ornament.
Standing high, think of falling;
holding a full cup, guard against spilling.
Keep this in mind and in heart,
and preserve for ever the constancy that brings good fortune.

keyLines.en: His merit stands higher than the great Shun, his diligence runs deeper than Yu the Great
keyLines.note: Compares Taizong with the sage-kings Shun and Yu, praising his achievement and his hard work.

keyLines.en: By arms he overcame disaster and disorder; by culture he cherished those from afar
keyLines.note: A summary of Taizong's rule: he put down disorder by force and won over distant peoples by civil virtue.

keyLines.en: People dig wells and drink, plough fields and eat
keyLines.note: A quotation from the old 'Song of the Earth-Striker': the people live so contentedly that they do not feel the ruler's power.

keyLines.en: The Way follows the season and is at ease; good fortune flows with the spring
keyLines.note: The Way of Heaven is open and clear, and good fortune flows on like the spring, a sign of a flourishing state.

keyLines.en: Standing high, think of falling; holding a full cup, guard against spilling
keyLines.note: The warning at the heart of the whole piece: one in a high position must remember the possibility of a fall, and one who is full must guard against overflowing.

glossary.en: ying qi - to receive the appointed time
glossary.note: To receive the mandate of Heaven.

glossary.en: deng san mai wu - to climb past the Three and go beyond the Five
glossary.note: To surpass the Three Sovereigns and the Five Emperors of legend.

glossary.en: wo ji dao ju - gripping the pivot and treading the square
glossary.note: To hold the key points of government and keep to the law.
Jewels and presents for a first meeting; here, tribute brought to the court.

glossary.en: gui tu feng ji - the tortoise chart and the phoenix chronicle
glossary.note: A tortoise carrying a diagram on its back and a phoenix marking the years are both legendary lucky signs.
The imperial carriage had a yellow silk canopy; here it stands for the throne.

glossary.en: zhen ji - constancy that brings good fortune
glossary.note: Holding to the right path and so gaining good fortune; the phrase comes from the Book of Changes (Yijing).

ming.background: This is the inscription part of the Jiuchenggong Liquan Ming (Inscription for the Sweet Spring at the Palace of Nine Perfections), written by Wei Zheng and copied by Ouyang Xun. Ouyang Xun was already over seventy, and his regular script is known for being steep, strong and exact; it is seen as the summit of regular script of the early Tang.
